cues.text: A Prince Born to the Church
Born on December 7, 521, at Gartan in County Donegal, Columba — baptized Colum, "the dove" — belonged to the powerful Uí Néill dynasty.
Descended on his father's side from the fourth-century High King Niall of the Nine Hostages, he belonged by birth among Ireland's most prominent families.
Rather than pursue the political prominence his royal blood might easily have secured him, Columba entered monastic training under St. Finnian at Moville.
There, he was ordained a deacon, beginning a religious formation that would eventually carry him far from the comfortable prospects his birth had offered.
A Battle, and an Exile Chosen as Penance
Columba's early religious career was marked by a controversy that became one of the most memorable episodes associated with his name.
It began as a dispute with St. Finnian over the right to keep a copy of a psalter Columba had transcribed.
The quarrel escalated into a battle between rival Irish factions at Cúl Dreimhne.
Troubled in conscience by the bloodshed his own involvement had helped provoke, Columba resolved to leave Ireland permanently.
This was whether under ecclesiastical sentence or, as many accounts suggest, through his own voluntary penance.
In exile, he vowed to win for Christ as many souls as had been lost in the battle he held himself responsible for.
Landfall at Iona
In 563, at forty-four years old, Columba crossed the sea with twelve companions in a small hide-covered currach, landing at Iona .
It was a small, remote island off Scotland’s western coast, granted to the monastic colonists, by most accounts, through Columba’s kinship ties to Dalriada’s ruling dynasty.
There the small community built a simple monastery of church, refectory, and cells from wattle and rough timber.
It was a humble beginning for what would become, within Columba's own lifetime, one of the most important centers of Christian learning and missionary activity in the whole of the British Isles.
Apostle to the Picts
From this modest island base, Columba undertook the great missionary labor of his life: the conversion of the Picts of northern Scotland, still almost entirely pagan.
Together with fellow Irish missionaries, he journeyed to the royal court of King Brude near Inverness.
Across more than three decades of patient evangelization, he gradually won an entire kingdom to the Christian faith.
He planted churches and monasteries throughout the Scottish mainland that would carry his influence for centuries after his death.
Scholar, Poet, and Statesman
Beyond his missionary labors, Columba was remembered by his own community and by later biographers as a man of remarkable range: a scholar and copyist of manuscripts.

He was also a poet of real skill in both Latin and his native Irish, and a statesman of sufficient standing to mediate disputes between kings and help negotiate the political status of the Irish colonists in Dalriada.
This combination of gifts made Iona, under his direction, not merely a monastery but a genuine center of civilization in a still-unsettled corner of the post-Roman world.
Legacy

Columba died at Iona on the night of June 8–9, 597, collapsing before the altar as the community gathered for the midnight office, surrounded, his biographer tells us, by disciples who caught him as he fell.
His feast is kept with particular devotion in both Scotland and Ireland.

For centuries after his death, Iona remained the mother-house of monasteries stretching across Scotland and Ireland alike—a light, as his earliest biographers called it, shining across the entire northern world.
It came from one small, wind-battered island that a penitent Irish prince had once chosen, in humility, as his place of exile.
A battle-scarred conscience, freely surrendered to God, had become, in the end, the founding stone of an entire nation's faith.
